transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. I came in because I just can't keep my mind on my actual experiments anymore. It's becoming a real problem at the lab. 

I'll be in the middle of an important grant call or a safety meeting, and I'll notice a pump vibrating, or one of the students will make some random side comment, or I'll suddenly think about an odd peak in an old spectrum. And then I'm just... gone. I'll go off chasing that one tiny detail for hours, completely sidetracked, while the actual work everyone needs from me just falls apart.
Have you struggled with this kind of distractibility and difficulty staying on task since you were a child, or is this a relatively new issue for you?

No, it's not something I've dealt with since I was a kid. It's actually a relatively new issue for me. I'd say this has been going on for about seven months now... basically right around the time I took over the multi-site spectroscopy project at work. Before that, I never really had a problem staying on task.
Beyond this difficulty with focus, have you been feeling particularly sad, hopeless, or unusually anxious since you started this new project?

No, I haven't really felt sad or hopeless. And I wouldn't say I'm unusually anxious, either. I mean, obviously it's frustrating when things fall apart at work, and that stresses me out, but... no, I don't feel depressed or panicked. It really just comes down to this complete inability to keep my train of thought where it needs to be.
Have you been experiencing any unusual or distressing events while you are asleep, such as night terrors or complex behaviors?
No, nothing like that. I don't have night terrors, and I haven't woken up doing anything strange or... complex, as you said. As far as I know, when I'm asleep, I'm just sleeping normally.
When you find yourself getting sidetracked by these details, do you ever feel like you are detached from your own body or that your surroundings feel dreamlike or unreal?

No, I haven't felt anything like that. I don't feel detached from my body, and things don't seem unreal or like a dream. It's really just that I get completely sidetracked and lose my focus. I'm definitely fully present and aware of my surroundings when it happens.
Have you been experiencing any physical symptoms, such as persistent fatigue, headaches, or body aches, that have worsened since you took on this new project?
No, I haven't noticed any physical symptoms like that. I'm not overly tired, and I haven't had any headaches or body aches. Physically, I feel fine. It's just the mental focus that's the problem.
When you are struggling to maintain your focus, does your mind feel particularly sluggish or exhausted, as if you are mentally drained?

No, it doesn't feel sluggish at all. If anything, it's the opposite. My mind feels... I guess, really active? It's definitely not exhausted or drained. I just can't seem to keep it pointed in one direction.

When you get sidetracked by those details, do you feel an internal pressure or a sense of 'must' that makes you feel like you have to investigate them, or is it more like your attention just naturally drifts away?

It's not really an internal pressure, no. I don't feel forced. It's more like my attention just gets completely hijacked and drifts off. Honestly, that's exactly why I came in—I just can't keep my mind on the actual experiment anymore. 

I could be right in the middle of an important grant call or a lab safety meeting, and I'll notice a pump vibration in the background, or a student will make a random side comment, or I'll suddenly think about some odd peak in an old spectrum... and that's it. My brain just goes there. Suddenly I'm off chasing that tiny detail for hours, while the actual work that everyone needs from me just completely falls apart.
If you were to step away from this multi-site spectroscopy project entirely, do you feel like your ability to focus would immediately return to how it was before?

I honestly don't know. I haven't really thought about just walking away from it. I mean, maybe? But the way my mind is right now, bouncing around so fast... I feel like even if I dropped the project, my brain would just find something else to latch onto and get distracted by. I don't think stepping away would just instantly fix how scattered I am.

When you took on this new multi-site spectroscopy project seven months ago, did it involve any significant negative changes, such as increased workload, interpersonal conflict, or feeling overwhelmed by new responsibilities?

No, not really. I mean, it was a big project to take on, sure, but it wasn't negative. I wasn't overwhelmed or having conflicts with anyone. It's just that... well, like I said, this whole thing with my mind being so scattered and active, it's been going on for about seven months now. It started right around the time I took over the multi-site spectroscopy project. So the timing lines up, but it wasn't because the project itself was bad or too much to handle.
Over the past seven months, have you noticed any periods where you felt unusually energetic, euphoric, or found that you needed significantly less sleep than usual while still feeling fully rested?

Yes, definitely the sleep part. Most nights I really only sleep maybe two or three hours. A lot of times I just fall asleep right on the couch with my laptop still open. 

But I don't wake up exhausted at all. I actually wake up completely sharp and ready to get right back to work. Honestly, it just feels like sleep is this inefficient interruption when I have so much going on.

During these periods where you have so much energy and need so little sleep, have you ever felt that you were receiving special messages, or that you were seeing or hearing things that others around you were not?

No, nothing like that. I haven't received any special messages or anything. And I definitely don't see or hear things that aren't there. 

I mean, my brain is going a million miles an hour with all the data and the logistics for the project, but it's just my own thoughts. They're just moving really, really fast. So, no, I haven't experienced anything like what you're asking about.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a distinct period of increased goal-directed activity, racing thoughts, and a significantly decreased need for sleep (2-3 hours) while maintaining high energy and sharpness, persisting for seven months. This pattern is consistent with a manic episode, and given the absence of depressive symptoms, F30.1 is the primary diagnosis.

diagnostic_checklist.duration_verified: Symptoms have been present for seven months.
